State-specific markups documented include Arkansas marking up all items 40-50%, Missouri inflating ramen by more than 65%, and Georgia marking up peanut butter over 70%. A bar of soap can cost up to $2.80 in prison, roughly 23 hours of work at the lowest wage.

raw_evidence.label: Prison wages: pennies per hour
raw_evidence.content: The buying power behind these prices is almost nothing. Wages for incarcerated workers nationally run roughly $0.14 to $0.63 per hour for most institutional jobs, and several states pay far less or nothing at all: Louisiana averages about $0.06 per hour, federal prison jobs pay about $0.12, and Texas pays its prison workers nothing. The Vera Institute documents wages as low as $0.06 to $0.24 per hour, with people working 6 to 8 hours a day, five days a week, yet earning only about $6 every two weeks. In Tennessee, wages of $0.17 to $0.50 per hour have not changed in over 30 years even as commissary prices track inflation. This is the benchmark that makes every commissary price in the dataset meaningful: a price of $1 is not $1 to someone earning six cents an hour.

raw_evidence.label: Vendors and kickback contracts
raw_evidence.content: Prison commissaries are often run by private vendors who pay the state a commission on every sale, an incentive structure that pushes prices up rather than down. Keefe Group (controlled by private-equity firm HIG Capital) and Union Supply Group are the dominant national vendors; the dataset records vendors including 'Keefe Commissary' (16 states), 'State-run' (17 states), and 'Union Supply Group' (6 states). Florida's DOC receives a 35.6% commission from Keefe under a five-year, $175 million contract. Kentucky receives a 16% kickback from Union Supply Group. These commissions mean the state profits more when incarcerated people pay more, aligning the interests of the prison and the vendor against the buyer.

raw_evidence.label: Vendors and kickback contracts
raw_evidence.content: Prison commissaries are often run by private vendors who pay the state a commission on every sale, an incentive structure that pushes prices up rather than down. Keefe Group (controlled by private-equity firm HIG Capital) and Union Supply Group are the dominant national vendors; the dataset records vendors including 'Keefe Commissary' (16 states), 'State-run' (17 states), and 'Union Supply Group' (6 states). Florida's DOC receives a 35.6% commission from Keefe under a five-year, $175 million contract. Kentucky receives a 16% kickback from Union Supply Group. These commissions mean the state profits more when incarcerated people pay more, aligning the interests of the prison and the vendor against the buyer.
